segments.text: Next up are physical incidents, which are comprised of fires, slips and falls, and musculoskeletal hazards.
If a fire starts, get everyone out. No hesitation.
Once the area is clear, if it's a small fire, grab the extinguisher and use the pass method.
Pull, aim, squeeze, and sweep.
Fires are classified into different types.
Class A, ordinary combustibles like paper and wood.
Class B, flammable liquids.
Class C, electrical.
Class D, metal fires.
Be sure to use the correct extinguisher for the type of fire.
If it's getting out of hand or you're unsure, don't take any chances.
Call for help.
After it's out, double check to make sure nothing can reignite.
Slips happen before you know it.
If you fall, don't jump up right away.
Take a second to see if you're okay.
If something hurts or you're feeling off, get help.
If you're fine, stand up slowly with support.
Then clean up whatever caused the fall so no one else gets hurt.
Musculoskeletal hazards are the aches that sneak up on you after repetitive work.
Whether it's your back, neck, or wrist, don't brush it off.
Stop, stretch, and adjust your setup.
If the pain keeps coming back, talk to someone about making changes and see a doctor before it turns into something bigger.
NFPA 45 is your guide to making sure fire safety is solid in the lab.
But don't just stop there. Local fire codes matter too.
So make sure you're on top of those.
Cutting corners here isn't worth the risk.
Now, when it comes to keeping your body in check, OSHA's got your back with regulations like 29 CFR 1910.900,
which focuses on preventing musculoskeletal disorders through better ergonomics.
And don't forget, standards like OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1450 for lab safety and 29 CFR 1910.38A for emergency plans are key to staying safe and compliant.
Get familiar with these and you'll be in good shape.
